<reason>A kept the debate anchored to the motion as written: the defect is tying basic coverage to work status, and that defect bites precisely when illness ends employment. B conceded the design flaw and defended patches, but A showed the patches (COBRA at full premium, means-tested Medicaid, churn and mid-treatment network changes) are friction-wrapped versions of public financing — and A's Q1 forced B to name subsidized exchange coverage as the worst-case exit, which A fairly converted into "every door opens into the same room." B landed the debate's sharpest hits (the "citing everything except single-payer" list-run, Vermont as revealed cost, the structural defense of Canada's ban) and its final-word closing was excellent, but those arguments proved transition difficulty and speculative systemic risk rather than end-state superiority — and B's embraced backstops face the same budget politics it weaponized. Taiwan survived as a live single-payer-with-supplemental example, blunting B's taxonomy win. A's clipped Rebuttal 2 and a premature "CON never answered Q1" jab were minor execution costs, not decisive. A's route to victory stayed cleaner and better matched to "preferable."</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The Q1 exchange decided the debate's shape: A pressured B to name a real exit for the 55-year-old with cancer; B honestly answered "subsidized exchange coverage," and A's closing converted that concession into the floor-vs-trapdoor frame. B's best counter-hit was the country list-run — "PRO defends single-payer by citing everything except single-payer" — damaging, but partially neutralized by Taiwan.</best_rebuttal>
